title: From Fourier Amplitudes to Persistence Images for Impact-Echo Defect Detection
summary: Impact-echo testing is a nondestructive testing method used to detect internal defects in concrete structures. However, boundary reflections, structured interference, and measurement noise can produce complex Fourier amplitude spectra, making defect classification difficult. We constructed a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude persistence image (FA-PI) from the Fourier amplitude spectrum. Using a fixed parameterization of exact multi-parameter persistent homology, each retained Fourier component is represented with frequency-bin location as one coordinate and amplitude as the other, and Gaussian kernels are then applied in this two-dimensional space. This construction has a direct analytical connection to the corresponding one-dimensional Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectrum. FA-PI was evaluated on an experimental backfill-void dataset and a public bridge-deck impact-echo dataset, and compared with raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier amplitude spectra using a linear classifier with a Softmax output and identical signal-level data splits. The evaluation included original signals and signals corrupted by Gaussian noise, sinusoidal interference, or mixed noise, with matching noise types and signal-to-noise ratios during training, validation, and testing. Performance was assessed using accuracy and macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score. Across the two datasets, FA-PI consistently outperformed the raw and Gaussian-smoothed Fourier baselines in the noisy-condition summaries. These findings indicate that representing Fourier spectral components in a two-dimensional frequency--amplitude space can improve impact-echo defect classification beyond frequency-axis smoothing alone.

title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
summary: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.

title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
summary: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.

title: Multi-Stream Residual Computation in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models reconstruct masked tokens in parallel, offering an alternative to autoregressive generation. Yet their Transformer backbones typically carry visible evidence and evolving masked predictions through a single residual stream. We equip masked diffusion models with multiple residual streams that persist through depth and adaptive routing between them, then investigate how they support these complementary roles. On the pretraining task, two streams reduce reconstruction perplexity by 5.71% on validation data and 5.13% on average across external corpora compared with standard residual connections. We observe that, without predefined roles, visible and masked positions learn distinct routing patterns. Causal interventions show that this distinction organizes read and write routing, while token-specific write strength remains important within each role. Guided by these findings, a model trained with role-conditioned routing recovers half the validation gain from adding a second stream. State interventions explain the benefit of the additional stream: it preserves early token representations for later reuse while evidence accumulates at masked positions. This mechanism recurs at a larger model scale, showing how persistent streams support context preservation alongside prediction refinement.

title: Read the Room Before Your Model Generates
summary: Large language models (LLMs) generally rely on sampling temperature to regulate the amount of randomness in their outputs. Mainstream methods for selecting temperature typically involve fixed, heuristic global settings and context or token-level calibration, rather than a geometrically interpretable representation of the communicative scenario. In this work, we introduce a simple and interpretable temperature selection framework, the \textbf{Scenario-Actor}, which adapts decoding to the inferred situational characteristics. Scenario-Actor extracts scenario-relevant structures from Transformer hidden states and determines the temperature from scenario embedding, a structured geometric representation of the communicative setting. Empirical results show that on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Scenario-Actor achieves strong goal-completion performance in interactive social scenarios, significant gains on open-ended instruction following, and competitive performance on multi-turn conversation compared to multiple baselines.

title: Recalibrating Many Questions with Few Labels: Minimax Rates and Identification Limits
summary: Many related prediction problems, which we call questions, come with few labels each. What information can be shared across them, and what is actually necessary for good decisions? We answer both for recalibration, motivated by decision models such as Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) that return a probability for any yes/no question a developer writes. A predictor reports a probability $P$ with output law $μ$ on $m$ questions, each with $n$ labels and a nondecreasing map $g_j(p)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid P=p)$; the compound risk is the excess Brier score over the true maps, averaged over questions. Over maps within sup-distance $τ\le 1$ and total variation $V\le 2$ of one nondecreasing shape (fixed effects), the minimax compound risk is $(mn)^{-2/3}+\min\{τ^2,1/n\}+\min\{τ^2,V^2,(V/n)^{2/3}\}$ up to universal constants, for every non-atomic $μ$. A pooled isotonic fit with a per-question correction sized once, on held-out labels of all questions, attains it without knowing $τ$, $V$ or $μ$ ($n\ge 2$, $m\ge 3$); tuning each question on its own labels loses a factor of order $\min\{n,\log(m^2/n)\}$ when the maps differ by constants and $m^2/n$ is large. When the maps are drawn from an unknown prior (random effects), other questions need not identify the Bayes rule. The loss, the identification regret, is at most $2^{-n}$ once the law of a question's data is known, extending a bound of Skibinsky (1968) for coins, and in the worst case at least $β_\star^{-n}/(72\sqrt{n})$ at every finite $m$, where $β_\star\approx 3.583$. Beyond a few labels per question, what cannot be learned is nearly unnecessary. For constant maps (an uninformative predictor) and constant-map priors, the exponential base is exactly $β_\star$, not the 4 suggested by the moment range; for monotone maps it lies in $[2,β_\star]$.

title: Convergence-Rate-Guided Algorithm Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization
summary: Expected improvement (EI) based on stochastic kriging (SK) surrogate is widely used in continuous simulation optimization, but unknown heteroscedastic noise on simulation output makes three basic design choices consequential: the incumbent used to define improvement, the replication level at each sampled point, and the terminal recommendation. Existing methods typically either assume the noise levels are known or choose these components separately through heuristic rules or empirical calibration. We instead derive a high-probability upper bound on the simple regret and systematically choose the three components within general rule classes to tighten this bound. We first establish a finite-sample confidence bound for the SK predictor with unknown and estimated noise levels as a foundation for the three design choices. We then analyze general posterior-quantile families for both the incumbent and the terminal recommendation. For the incumbent, minimizing the regret bound selects a lower quantile coefficient that matches the coefficient in the SK predictor confidence bound. For the terminal recommendation, minimizing the same bound instead selects the sampled point with the best upper posterior quantile under the same coefficient. These opposite quantile choices reflect the different roles of search and implementation in simulation optimization. Intermediate simulations are exploratory with an optimistic incumbent, while the terminal recommendation is implemented in the real system and is therefore relatively conservative about the remaining posterior uncertainty. Under mild conditions satisfied by common kernels, minimizing a tractable kernel-specific bound yields $Θ(\log T)$ replications. To our knowledge, this is the first simple-regret guarantee for a continuous-domain EI-type simulation optimization method that learns unknown heteroscedastic variances through replications.

title: On the Optimality of Random Features under General Conditions: Misspecified Cases and Robust Learning
summary: Random features provide a standard approach to scaling kernel methods to large datasets by approximating the kernel with a finite-dimensional feature map. Existing works of random feature methods primarily focus on well-specified models and light-tailed noise conditions, leaving a gap in understanding their performance under more general conditions, such as misspecified models and heavy-tailed noise. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of kernel ridge regression with random features (KRR-RF) under general conditions. In the light-tailed noise setting, we improve upon the worst-case uniform bounds of the feature map used in the previous works and lead to the minimax optimal learning rates with $2r+γ>α_0$, where $(r,γ,α_0)$ denote the regularity of the target function, the effective dimension of the kernel, and the embedding index of the RKHS, respectively. In the heavy-tailed noise setting, we leverage a recently developed Hilbert-valued Fuk-Nagaev inequality and extend the same optimal results under finite weak moment conditions. The additional cost to achieve robustness is a mildly stronger explicit sample-size requirement than in the light-tailed case. For both settings, our results recover the conditions random features budgets (up to log factors) required in the previous works. In the most benign case when $α_0=γ$, KRR-RF are minimax optimal for all $r \in (0,1]$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to establish optimal learning rates for KRR-RF under weak moment conditions in the misspecified setting. Numerical experiments and a real data analysis validate the derived learning rates and demonstrate their practical relevance in the presence of mis-specification and heavy-tailed noise.

title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
summary: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).

title: ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

title: Bayesian Test-Time Inference of Task-Aligned Similarity from Weak Interactive Feedback
summary: Language model systems repeatedly make test-time decisions by comparing similarity: they retrieve exemplars, rank candidates, and revise responses. Yet similarity is not unique: lexical, semantic, structural, and stylistic resemblance can point to different candidates, and the task-aligned notion can change across instances. We introduce BASIS (Bayesian Axis Selection via Interactive Signals), a training-free Bayesian method that uses weak test-time feedback to infer which criterion in a supplied, task-specific library governs the current decision. It maintains a joint posterior over candidate targets and criteria, updates it from scalar scores, pairwise preferences, or verifier outputs, and selects probes by expected information gain. In a finite noisy model, we characterize when the target-criterion pair is recoverable and show why fixed-criterion and fixed-mixture rules can fail under criterion shift. Across concept recovery, reasoning exemplar selection, and response refinement, BASIS improves six-probe concept-recovery Success@1 from 56.0% to 68.1%, reasoning accuracy from 72.3% to 73.1%, and refinement win rate from 61.4% to 63.8% over tuned static mixtures. It also exceeds compute-matched best-of-N selection on reasoning (72.1%) and refinement (61.2%). Gains are largest under criterion mismatch and with larger candidate pools, and matched controls indicate that adaptive criterion weighting explains much of the benefit, with joint target-criterion inference adding further value. BASIS selects only among supplied criteria and does not discover new ones.

title: LLM Agents for Automated Post-Training via Structured Recipe Optimization
summary: Automated post-training transforms pre-trained large language models (LLMs) into models capable of handling diverse domains by automatically constructing and optimizing a recipe of coupled decisions over data sources, data processing, cross-domain composition, and training configuration under a limited experimental budget. Existing automation either searches predefined recipe spaces that enable systematic optimization but remain fixed rather than adapting their available choices to the target tasks, or uses open-ended agents that discover task-specific choices but leave them implicit in trial-level edits, limiting their systematic reuse and recombination across trials. To fill this gap, we introduce optimization over a task-adapted recipe space, a novel paradigm that can adapt the recipe space itself to the target tasks while representing its choices explicitly for systematic reuse, recombination, and joint optimization. We instantiate this paradigm with Structured Recipe Optimization (SRO), comprising an LLM-based Recipe-Space Designer that constructs the task-adapted recipe space and a Multi-Domain Recipe Optimizer that uses structured trial evidence to guide LLM candidate construction and multi-objective Bayesian trial selection. Extensive experiments show that SRO achieves the highest average score in all evaluated target-model and agent-LLM combinations. In joint post-training across three capability domains and six benchmarks, SRO reaches 41.1 versus 15.4 for the strongest baseline on Qwen3-1.7B with GPT-5.4, and 53.8 versus 40.8 on Qwen3-4B with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Our code is available at https://github.com/RuohLiuq/SRO.

title: Graph Metanetworks for Transformer Based Language Models
summary: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. Importantly, their weight space has a richer symmetry group: beyond neuron permutations, attention introduces continuous general-linear symmetries of the attention matrices and permutations of entire heads. Existing methods for transformer weights either capture only part of these symmetries or are restricted to a single, fixed architecture, and none accounts for language-model-specific components such as the token embeddings. Building on graph metanetworks, we propose a graph-based approach that is both symmetry-aware and applicable across depths and widths. We formalize a weight-space symmetry group of complete decoder-only language models and provide a graph construction that is invariant to it. We further introduce two new transformer-population datasets with novel tasks, such as training-corpus prediction and fine-tuning detection, on which our approach notably outperforms existing baselines.

title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.

title: Not All Drift Is a Mechanism: Tracing Prompt Adaptation in LLMs
summary: Prompt-based adaptation offers several ways to specialize a frozen language model, ranging from natural-language prompt optimization to learned continuous prompts. These methods are usually compared through downstream performance, although similar outputs need not arise from similar internal computations. We study how discrete prompt optimization, prompt tuning, and prefix tuning alter the processing of dense and mixture-of-experts language models. Our analysis shows that the location of the adaptation predicts how task information is carried to the output: optimized text primarily changes response construction, input-level prompts write their influence into content representations, and layer-wise prefixes maintain direct control through attention. In MoE models, these differences further induce distinct expert-routing patterns. At the same time, common representation-level measurements respond strongly to generic context changes and do not reliably distinguish useful adaptations from matched placebos. We argue that understanding prompt adaptation requires separating representation drift from the part of that drift that is aligned with, and causally used by, the model's task computation. This perspective provides practical guidance for selecting, evaluating, and interpreting prompt adaptation methods.

title: PRISM: Calibrating Black-Box Judges with Counterfactual Probes
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as judges to reduce reliance on costly human evaluation, yet their scores can systematically disagree with human judgments. We ask whether responses to an explicitly imposed evaluative bias can help correct a judge's implicit scoring biases. We introduce PRISM (Probe-based Residual Inference of Scoring Misalignment), which holds the evaluated content fixed and measures score changes when attributes are emphasized or de-emphasized. A local sensitivity model motivates representing these responses as a surrogate Jacobian. Ridge regression on human labels learns a correction to the baseline score. The resulting scoring protocol is rubric-free: it uses overall scores without requesting criterion-level ratings. In the main Jev and Sol comparisons on SummEval summarization and HANNA story evaluation, PRISM and its learned-baseline variant significantly improve agreement with human rankings over uncalibrated scores while remaining competitive with rubric-based methods. A controlled SummEval comparison yields similar agreement for rubric-derived quality probes and style probes, supporting calibration without reproducing rubric criteria. The learned coefficients reveal shared and opposing correction directions across judges.

title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
summary: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.

title: BLADE: Auditing Information Use for Failure Attribution in LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model multi-agent systems extend individual agents' capabilities through collaboration across specialized roles, tools, and workflows. Yet collaboration makes failures harder to diagnose: one agent may misinterpret a correct result while others carry the mistake forward. Failure attribution therefore seeks to identify the responsible agent and decisive error step. Recent methods trace dependencies, but knowing where information came from is not the same as knowing where it went wrong. We introduce BLADE (Blame Localization via Audited Dependency Evidence), a training-free framework that moves beyond tracing information to auditing its use. Using Jev for structured probabilistic judgments, BLADE uses dependency probabilities to select relevant source-decision handoffs for auditing. At these handoffs, it examines whether receiving decisions use their sources faithfully and within task requirements, distinguishing error introduction, propagation, and repair. These findings inform a global diagnosis that considers all execution steps. Without reference answers, BLADE achieves the best or tied-best step accuracy among eight strategies under a shared Jev decision interface on 1,228 failed runs across five Who&When and Who&When Pro subsets, outperforming All-at-once by 2.2-11.1 percentage points. Making responsibility evidence explicit offers a path toward more interpretable and reliable agentic systems.

title: Beyond Answer Voting: Fine-Grained Correction of LLM Reasoning through Graph Alignment across Sampled Traces
summary: Large language models increasingly tackle tasks that require multi-step reasoning, where errors in intermediate claims can affect the final answer. Self-consistency (SC) improves reasoning by voting over sampled final answers, but its vote leaves intermediate disagreements unresolved. To address this problem, we introduce DDRG (Disagreement-Driven Verification Guided by Reasoning Graphs), a framework for selective correction from a frozen bank of reasoning traces. Our insight is that graph alignment can expose claim-level disagreements and provide correction evidence without expanding the sampled trace bank. DDRG builds source-grounded claim graphs and sends localized conflicts to an answer-blind verifier. A verifier-supported refutation that reaches the majority answer's supporting path triggers one focused repair; otherwise, DDRG returns the exact SC vote. Experimental results across five benchmarks show that native zero-shot DDRG improves macro-average accuracy over direct answering by 8.65 and 15.83 percentage points for Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B. It also exceeds CoT, the evaluated GoT and GoV question-answering adaptations, and SC on this macro metric. DDRG links local verification to selective correction without enlarging the initial candidate bank.

title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
summary: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in $3$ of $7$ (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average $98\%$ of its score across the other four.

title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.

title: Simultaneous Inference for Centre-Outward Rankings of Random Objects
summary: In many applications one object is chosen to represent a sample and the least typical objects are set aside, usually without any measure of uncertainty. We measure how central an object is by its reference depth, the probability that a random reference point is closer to it than to a random opponent. Using only pairwise dissimilarities, we construct simultaneous intervals for all ranks, a centre set that contains the most central observation under stated conditions, and outlier sets that contain only objects among the least central ones, each with asymptotic probability at least a prescribed level. These guarantees hold even though the ranked objects are themselves random. For symmetric distributions on the real line, the centre set has the smallest possible order of size up to a logarithmic factor, and in dimension three or more it reduces to the most central observation with probability tending to one. For typical meteorological years the centre set usually contains several candidate years, so the data do not determine the year on which building-energy simulations rest; for three collections of gene trees it contains one tree, whose features can be reported as those of the most central tree.

title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents
summary: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent's continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. title: On the Monitorability of Natural Language Autoencoders: Identification vs Discrimination
summary: Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs) are proposed as oversight tools for language models: an Activation Verbaliser (AV) writes an English explanation of an activation vector, and an Activation Reconstructor (AR) maps the explanation back to a vector. Their value for oversight depends on a human monitor being able to tell a true account of an activation from a false one, given the Av's explanation. We formalise NLA training and NLA oversight deployment as two different referential games from Emergent Communication: training is a generative referential game, while oversight is a discriminative, multi-modal, partially-observable referential game played over a many-to-many relation between the monitored language model's activations and the accounts that are true of them. The gap between the two games predicts that AV's explanations will identify which activation they describe without discriminating its true account from closely matched false ones, since training never asks explanations to rule anything out. Using the NLA's own AR as a maximally-sympathetic surrogate monitor model, we experimentally confirm this theoretical insight on one released checkpoint: true accounts beat accounts of other activations in all 320 comparisons, but beat fluent rivals differing in a single claim only 60.2% of the time (std.err. 6.7%, chance at 50%, $n = 35$). A meaning-preserving rewrite by an uninvolved model costs only 2.1% of the distance to another activation's account, so the failure is not due to the NLA pair having developed private conventions in the AV's explanations. Our rival accounts test only transcript-level truths, which the monitored language model's conversation settles, so these results bound the easiest case and leave claims about the monitored model's own processing untested. We state conjectures that would make both results consequences of the framework.

title: SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics
summary: Frontier language-model agents can now improve robots on their own: they write control code, test it, and keep what works as skills and memories for the next task. We introduce SEAR (Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics), a framework and benchmark built around two questions. Is the agent really learning, or just trying more often? And does what it learns still help on new tasks, in a new simulator, and on a real robot? The framework runs an agent in three modes: it writes code that becomes the policy (code-as-policy), acts live in the control loop (agent-as-policy), or works as a researcher that fine-tunes a vision-language-action model (auto-research). The benchmark adds controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts, familiar tasks, privileged simulator state, larger budgets, and luck. Across seven frontier language models, 330 simulated and five physical tasks, and over four years of agent runtime, we highlight three findings. First, the learning curve of a robotic agent depends both on the overall time budget and the task difficulty relative to model capability. Harder tasks make longer sessions worthwhile; on easier tasks, re-rolling short attempts does just as well. Second, control code and shared routines transfer across tasks and simulators, while task-specific solutions do not. On a real robot, we observe a performance gap between agent-designed practice and novel human-designed scenes. Third, different models evolve more effectively in different ways. Some do best acting live, others writing code first. And a text-only model keeps pace with a comparable multimodal one: perception helps with error assessment, but agentic reasoning and tool use can matter more. We release the benchmark and codebase to support future research.

summary: LLM ensemble gains are often measured against a single baseline, but the value attributed to additional candidates can change with the comparison used. We study an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions: Direct (no candidates), Single-slot (one candidate in a multi-slot interface), Duplicate (one candidate repeated), and Multi-candidate (separately generated candidates). Under either non-diverse control, overall candidate gain (CIV) splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast (DSV) and a candidate-context contrast (CCV); the split, but not CIV, depends on the chosen control. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2), the repetition gap Rep=-8.33 pp [-13.25, -3.75] quantifies the difference between gains measured against Duplicate and Single-slot. On a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200, k=3, aggregator output limit 4096), paired Delta Rep=+9.67 pp [+6.00, +13.50]; within panels, Rep changes sign (original -6.33; stronger +3.33). title: Looking Complete Is Not Being Grounded: Evaluating LLM Sitreps Against Human-Authored Situation Reports
summary: Evaluation for automatic crisis reporting should measure what practitioners need, not what is convenient to compare. Through LLM-assisted, author-approved content analysis, we derive a 15-slot information schema from professional humanitarian situation reports using qualitative content analysis, then evaluate 121 human and 261 LLM-generated reports across five disasters and three hazard types. Under google/gemini-3.7-flash on Cyclone Idai, the best machine arm is nominally above the empirical human ceiling (0.827 vs. 0.821), but the difference is statistically indistinguishable from zero (95\% bootstrap CI $[-.049,.059]$; permutation $p=.852$), and the ordering does not replicate under openai/gpt-5.6-luna. On a blind 100-item Idai sample, the author agrees with the Gemini judge at 0.910 accuracy and unweighted Cohen's $κ=.799$. All four judges clear the plan's raw-agreement criterion of .7; only Gemini reaches .7 on chance-corrected $κ$. Across the three primary events, machine reports reproduce 5.4-11.0% of same-day official figures. Across those same events, raw exact-number matching links 14.3-19.6% of official figures and 85.4-90.1% of machine figures to the social stream; manual audit confirms 45/50 declared absences, 4/25 official matches, and 24/25 machine matches semantically. The issuing-provenance gap is positive in all 12 observed event-judge cells: report date, organisation, series, and authority were not supplied at professional-report coverage in any cell. title: From Relation-Specific Heads to Shared Interventions: Contextual Entrainment in Language Models
summary: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.

title: Reliable Memory from Unstable Growth: Curating Self-Written Agent Playbooks with Randomized Experiments
summary: Persistent textual memory lets language-model agents reuse lessons from past tasks to improve on future multi-step tasks without retraining. Systems such as ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet keep it as a playbook: lessons the agent writes after each task and reads in its prompt. A key challenge is to decide which lessons improve later tasks. Current systems leave the decision to the agent itself, which makes performance unstable: the same procedure can write a playbook that helps or one that falls up to 69.6 points below no playbook. These findings motivate valuing lessons by their measured effect on task success rather than by the agent's judgment. We propose Randomized Block Curation (RBC), which measures this effect with a randomized experiment on practice tasks. It groups related lessons into blocks large enough to move success measurably and, on each practice task, includes or leaves out every block at random. Random inclusion makes tasks with and without a block comparable, so the gap in their success estimates the block's effect. RBC keeps the blocks that help and, since the same procedure can write a helpful or a harmful playbook, grows several and serves whichever curated, whole or no playbook scores best on fresh practice episodes. Across two memory systems, three models and three benchmarks, RBC raises average success to 66.9, against 55.5 with the whole playbook, 54.1 with no playbook and 53.8 when the agent's own judgment picks the lessons to keep.

title: Who Improves the Robot? Toward Physical Recursive Self-Improvement
summary: Robots are increasingly autonomous in task execution, yet their improvement remains largely human-driven. This study investigates Physical Recursive Self-Improvement (Physical RSI), in which physical experience guides lasting updates to both a robot's capabilities and its improvement procedure, making subsequent improvement more effective across tasks. Physical RSI faces challenges from noisy observations, continuous dynamics, costly trials, and irreversible consequences. We present an L0-L5 framework that differentiates capability-level from meta-level updates and within-task from across-task gains, reserving L5 for independently verified recursive gain. We study existing methods around harness adaptation and model training, alongside safety and control mechanisms that govern execution and successive updates. Our analysis reveals that, despite substantial progress in self-improvement, the surveyed literature does not yet demonstrate Physical RSI as defined by our framework. We identify research priorities in reliable feedback, causal attribution, safety preservation, and benchmarking, outlining a path toward robots that autonomously improve how they learn while ensuring safety. The GitHub repository for Physical RSI is available at https://github.com/SAIL-Research-Lab/Physical-RSI.

title: Fast Rates for Offline Q-Learning with KL Regularization
summary: This paper investigates offline Q-learning for finite-horizon Markov decision processes with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. Recent studies have shown that KL regularization can yield fast rates in offline decision-making problems. However, it remains unclear whether Q-learning, which adopts incremental stochastic approximation updates, can achieve such fast rates in the offline setting. We first propose KL-regularized Q-Learning (KLQ), a simple variant of classical Q-learning. By exploiting KL regularization, we prove that KLQ achieves a sample complexity of $\widetilde{O}(1/ε)$ without explicit pessimism. This guarantee, however, has an exponential dependence on the KL regularization parameter and the horizon. To address this limitation, we further propose KL-regularized Pessimistic Q-Learning (KLPQ), which incorporates pessimism into KLQ. We prove that KLPQ retains the same \(\widetilde O(1/ε)\) rate while removing the explicit exponential dependence, thereby further improving the sample complexity. To the best of our knowledge, these results establish the first fast-rate guarantees for offline Q-learning in tabular finite-horizon KL-regularized MDPs.

title: Texture Interpolation as Texton Matching
summary: Texture interpolation asks what should lie between two textures. Standard methods typically blend pixels or features at corresponding spatial locations, implicitly assuming that co-located elements should be mixed. For unrelated textures, however, this correspondence is arbitrary: a crack at one location has no particular relationship to a fiber at the same location in another image. We study whether this hidden pairing choice is itself a major determinant of interpolation quality. We represent textures as collections of local appearance vectors, or textons, and replace positional pairing with appearance-aware matching while keeping the encoder, representation, and decoder fixed. This isolates the effect of correspondence from changes in model capacity or training. Across texture pairs, appearance-aware matching consistently improves the distributional quality of interpolated midpoints over positional feature blending. Soft matching produces the strongest midpoint statistics, whereas one-to-one assignments yield more balanced transitions and closer agreement with the target endpoint. The same intervention also improves a second pretrained texture interpolator without retraining. These results identify correspondence as a first-class design choice in texture interpolation: meaningful transitions depend not only on how strongly two textures are mixed, but also on which local appearances are mixed with one another.

title: Can an Agent Learn to Predict Its Own Failure? Outcome-Grounded Confidence Calibration in LLM Agents
summary: Controlling an acting LLM agent means deciding, at each step of a long-horizon task, whether to trust its next action, abstain, or hand off to a human. That decision needs a per-step confidence signal predicting whether the current rollout will eventually succeed. The agent's own self-reported verbalized confidence is the natural candidate, but existing reinforcement learning methods calibrate it against the correctness of a decision at the current step. We propose a method to calibrate it against the eventual outcome of a multi-step episode: under GRPO, the group of rollouts for a task supplies success labels, and a proper scoring rule scores each step's confidence against the realized outcome. In offline RL on recorded trajectories of a Qwen2.5-7B agent in ALFWorld, TextWorld, and WebShop environments, the AUROC of step confidence against episode outcome rises from near chance to 0.68-0.85, and the top-10% of steps the agent is most confident about succeed ~4.3x more often than average. In online RL on the live ALFWorld agent, four calibration rewards improve early-step AUROC, expected calibration error goes from 0.42 to below 0.12, and selective execution improves over both the untrained agent and a format-only RL control, without degrading task success. We also introduce an evaluation protocol that separates episode depth, task difficulty, and attempt-level foresight, which shows where the gain lies: the trained agent recognizes from its first step which tasks it will fail, while telling a succeeding attempt from a failing one at the same task is harder, with some early-window signal emerging on TextWorld.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped SGD with Linear Decay
summary: In this paper, we study the last-iterate convergence of clipped stochastic gradient descent under heavy-tailed noise. We assume that the stochastic gradients are unbiased and that the noise has a bounded central $p$-th moment, where $1<p\le2$. For smooth convex objectives, a linearly decreasing learning rate gives a high-probability error bound of order $O(LR^2\log(1/δ)/T+σR(\log(1/δ)/T)^{(p-1)/p})$. We further establish last-iterate guarantees for nonsmooth composite objectives and smooth composite objectives with proximal updates. In addition, when a causal adversary replaces at most $q$ gradients, the same clipped update achieves a bound with $\log(1/δ)$ replaced by $\log(1/δ)+q$. The corresponding lower bounds for the clean and corrupted oracle models are also provided.

title: Approximating Optimal Policies in Heterogeneous Asynchronous Multi-player Bandits
summary: Motivated by applications to cognitive radio networks, multi-player multi-armed bandits (MMAB) have attracted considerable attention in recent years. The asynchronous variant, in which players are active only at a fraction of timesteps, better reflects real-world decentralized networks, where devices are not permanently active. Despite its practical relevance, this setting remains relatively understudied. Existing work on asynchronous MMAB has focused on homogeneous players, who share the same activation probability, a setting in which the optimal centralized allocation can be easily characterized. In contrast, efficiently computing the optimal allocation in the heterogeneous setting, where players have different activation probabilities, has remained an open problem. In this work, we investigate this problem and first establish its NP-hardness. We then turn to the greedy algorithm, which runs in polynomial time, and prove that it achieves a $\frac{1}{e}$-approximation of the optimal allocation. Furthermore, when players are processed in decreasing order of their activation probabilities, the approximation guarantee improves to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}}$. Overall, our results establish the greedy algorithm as an efficient approximation to the optimal allocation, providing a practical oracle baseline for the design of online algorithms for heterogeneous asynchronous multi-player bandits.

title: FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
summary: Large-scale expert parallelism (EP) has become the standard deployment configuration for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models in production. Meanwhile, the highly dynamic nature of LLM workloads requires providers to continuously adjust serving capacity to match fluctuating demand. Scaling MoE serving cannot be efficiently achieved by simply adding or removing serving instances; instead, it often requires resizing the EP group within an existing instance, which we refer to as intra-instance scaling.Existing inference engines primarily rely on instance-level scaling, which destroys and reconstructs entire serving instances, incurring substantial scaling overhead.   We present FastEEP (Fast Elastic Expert Parallel), a fast intra-instance scaling system for MoE serving based on the principle of Partial Reuse. FastEEP reuses existing runtime state across worker execution, GPU memory, and communication by separating reusable execution structures from the resources activated by the current EP configuration. This separation enables coordinated resource reclamation and reconfiguration while preserving costly-to-reconstruct state, allowing fast EP scaling without full instance teardown and reconstruction. Our evaluation shows that FastEEP achieves 4.5x--11.7x faster scaling than the existing vLLM-based approach across different models, enabling efficient, fine-grained scaling of MoE serving.

title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting: Continual Learning for Radar Waveform Classification
summary: Automated radar waveform recognition classifies the waveform and modulation type of a received signal. As new waveform variants appear over time, a deployed classifier must learn them without retraining from scratch. Catastrophic Forgetting occurs when learning new waveforms overwrites prior knowledge. Continual Learning (CL) methods tackle this challenge, but prior radar studies only evaluate a few methods on narrow benchmarks. Practitioners lack evidence on which method to deploy or which mechanisms are effective. This work presents the first large-scale benchmark of continual learning for radar waveform recognition. Eighteen CL methods are evaluated on a sequential ten-task problem, drawn from four public datasets spanning 54 waveforms, under task- and class-incremental (TIL, CIL) settings and single- and multi-epoch regimes. Methods that retain data from old tasks lead both TIL and CIL settings. Plain replay alone closes 77-88% of the gap between the lower and upper practical limits under TIL, but only 46-55% under CIL. The internal mechanisms of the leading methods are ablated and statistically tested to identify effective mechanisms. Each ablation is paired against its full method over n=6 training seeds, topped up to n=12 when inconclusive, and p-values are Holm-Bonferroni corrected within each method's family. Ablation results show that several mechanisms confer smaller but statistically significant gains. Combining these mechanisms improves the leading F1 score by 3.4-5.5% and 2.7-4.9% under TIL and CIL, respectively, and the combined models exceed every benchmarked method in both settings for all SNRs. These results give researchers of radar waveform classification systems a mechanism-level basis for design.

title: Beyond RMSE and Granger Gain: Multi-Horizon Forecast-Error Entropy for Nonlinear Predictive Coupling
summary: We investigate whether the past of an auxiliary time series provides predictive information about a target beyond that contained in the target's own history. We compare matched out-of-sample target-only and target-plus-source forecasts and introduce the forecast-error distribution entropy (FEDE) predictive-causality framework, where predictive causality is understood in the Granger sense: auxiliary history is informative when it improves prediction beyond the target's own past. FEDE quantifies how the full signed forecast-error distribution changes across prediction horizons. Controlled nonlinear benchmarks hide source-target dependence behind nonlinear transformations not supplied to the predictors. LightGBM recovers these hidden channels, whereas Ridge does not. Across four equal-power nonlinearities and four noise levels, the mean response-sensitivity statistic for FEDE remains 29.00, 27.47, 23.22, and 28.67, compared with 14.09, 10.68, 12.67, and 12.71 for mean log-RMSE gain. Directional and source controls separate the true source-to-target channel from the reverse direction and from independent periodic, quasiperiodic, chaotic, and autoregressive auxiliaries. Chronological Granger-style comparisons show strong model-form dependence: a degree-2 polynomial model is exceptionally sensitive to the matched quadratic channel but becomes weak or oppositely aligned for other nonlinearities, while basic convergent cross mapping is weak or directionally inconsistent in this stochastic, partly non-invertible setting. FEDE remains positively aligned across all 108 tested combinations of window length, history length, and maximum forecast horizon. Together, these results establish FEDE as a sensitive and robust horizon-resolved tool that extracts predictive information beyond conventional error-magnitude measures when the nonlinear interaction form is unknown. title: Judges Follow the Reference: The Derivation Gap in Verifying Tool-Call Arguments
summary: Tool-call judges evaluate argument values proposed by LLM agents. We find that they accept a correct value less often when their input holds no reference for it, that is, no text that says what the value should be. This happens when the value is a default value from the function schema that the user did not mention, when it has to be inferred, or when the text it comes from was cut from the judge input. We call this drop in acceptance the derivation gap. It appears across all seven judges we evaluate, including System One models CLM and Jev. The gap is not only a truncation artifact: correct default values have the largest gap on a benchmark with no truncation. A controlled source-relocation test shows that judges follow the reference in their input: they favor a visible incorrect value over a correct value whose source is hidden. We introduce DeRef (Derived Reference): a separate model reads the full history without seeing the candidate and writes a reference for the judge. Across three benchmarks, DeRef improves overall argument AUROC for all judges tested. On the controlled test, it raises AUROC from chance or below to between 98.40 and 99.59.

title: Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal
summary: Although language is predominantly spoken, empirical tests of surprisal theory rely almost entirely on written text. In practice, surprisal is estimated using language models (LMs) trained on text and applied to transcriptions, creating a text bottleneck that limits evaluation of the theory in the spoken modality. We remove this bottleneck by estimating surprisal directly from the speech signal using a speech LM. This raises a key question: should surprisal be defined over realization-specific acoustic inputs or over abstract linguistic units? Since a single unit can have many distinct acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by the model, defining surprisal over abstract units is difficult. To address this, we introduce an importance sampling estimator that approximates the probability of an abstract unit by marginalizing over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model. Using pupillometry data from a listening study, we evaluate surprisal theory in this text-free setting at multiple levels of granularity. title: Pin It on Anyone: Certified Targeted Displacement of Multi-Bit LLM Watermarks Without the Key
summary: Multi-bit watermarking embeds a message, typically an account identifier, into LLM output so that harmful text can be traced to its origin. We show an attack technique that allows to alter the watermarking message. This allows to, for example, exchange the embedded account ID to an arbitrary different one. The attacker mainly needs access to a few accounts for generating LLM output and model logits, but crucially not the secret key used to watermark. The attacker then rewrites the text, keeping its meaning, so that the watermarking message decoder recovers the watermarking message embedded by the attacker. We are, to our knowledge, the first to propose such an attack, which we call a targeted displacement. Theoretically, we present upper and lower bounds on the probability of our attack succeeding. This bound depends on the number of accounts the attacker has access to, the length of the message and some characteristics of the given text. Our attack can succeed whenever we can bound the ambiguity of the generated text well enough. Empirically, we test our attack technique against five watermarking methods and four LLMs. Attack success tracks our predicted bounds, allowing us to alter watermarking messages in almost all cases with high accuracy, given enough accounts. title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
summary: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(φ^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.

title: DoubtLess: Training-Free Contrastive Decoding for Efficient Reasoning
summary: Reasoning models achieve strong performance through long chains of thought (CoT), but often spend more tokens than needed to solve a problem. Existing ways to shorten the CoT require additional training for each model, add a fixed steering vector to the model's hidden states, or use decoding heuristics such as stopping early or banning words like "wait", which can reduce accuracy. We propose DoubtLess, a training-free decoding method in which a much smaller reasoning model steers the large one towards brevity. The small model reads the large model's CoT so far twice, once prompted to be brief (the brief thinker) and once prompted to be verbose (the verbose thinker), and the difference between its two logit vectors, scaled by a strength, is added to the large model's logits at every step of the CoT. On seven benchmarks of competition mathematics, graduate-level science and competitive programming, DoubtLess shortens the CoT of Qwen3-32B by 31% with unchanged accuracy, outperforming five inference-time baselines. We also show that DoubtLess reduces thinking tokens per turn by 20% in a self-debugging coding agent with unchanged task performance. It also generalizes to two other model families with unchanged accuracy. When combined with training-based compression, it further shortens the CoT of a model already trained for brevity. Ablations and behavioral analysis show that DoubtLess reduces repeated checking, with most token savings coming after the correct answer first appears in the CoT. title: Scaling Online Optimal Transport Minibatches for Flow Matching
summary: A central challenge in scaling flow models is maintaining stability in training and integration. In flow matching, this stability depends critically on how source samples are paired with data. Independent random pairing introduces substantial stochasticity, motivating minibatch optimal transport (OT) to construct online source-target couplings that reduce this randomness (Tong et al., 2024). However, as applications extend to larger and higher-dimensional datasets, small minibatches can limit these benefits, while scaling the coupling to substantially larger minibatches at every iteration is computationally prohibitive. Moreover, how OT coupling affects the full stochastic gradient and integration remains theoretically unresolved. In this work, we develop a scalable online entropic OT approximation that enables substantially larger source-target couplings while preserving the benefits of OT. We close the theoretical gap for both unregularized and entropic OT by proving strict reductions in full stochastic-gradient variance and integration error relative to independent pairing, and further characterize how these improvements strengthen as the online coupling minibatch grows. Experiments on single-cell gene interpolation-flow and image-flow training validate these predictions, showing that larger online couplings consistently improve training stability and final generation performance.

title: Learning When to Transfer: Reinforcement Learning for Carbon-Footprint Modeling in New Manufacturing Domains
summary: Manufacturers often need to characterize a new material, process, or product before enough operating data are available to train reliable predictive models for this new, target domain. Existing manufacturing operations contain potentially useful knowledge to accelerate this characterization, but indiscriminate reuse of data from existing source domains can cause negative transfer in learning of the new, target domain when the manufacturing domains differ sufficiently. This work proposes a reinforcement-learning method for selective knowledge transfer, where its reward scores each opportunity to transfer against supervised alternatives, so negative transfer is avoided and controlled during forward prediction instead of being diagnosed afterwards. Given limited data from a new target domain, the learned policy chooses among predictors based on individual source operations, subsets of the sources, or the supervised alternatives: fully pooled sources, or target data alone. A validation gate deploys the transferred prediction only when it improves upon the supervised alternatives. We demonstrate the approach by quantifying the embodied greenhouse-gas emissions of parts produced via material-extrusion additive manufacturing, using data from 729 experiments spanning five materials: ABS, PETG, TPU, PLA, and recycled PLA. The response combines measured fabrication electricity with polymer-specific cradle-to-gate production factors, while 22 material, process, and toolpath features characterize each experiment. In leave-one-material-out evaluation, this method achieves a mean test RMSE of 5.2 g CO2e per part, 20.00% lower than target-only training (32.5% lower when only 5-10% of the target training data are available) and 10.30% lower than indiscriminate source-target pooling.

title: Knowing the User Is Not Knowing What We Established: Grounding Awareness in Personal Agents
summary: Personal-agent memory has largely focused on learning what users know, prefer, and want. However, knowing the user does not necessarily mean knowing what the user and the agent have established together. An assistant's proposal should not become an authorized instruction merely because it is remembered. We introduce Grounding Awareness, the ability to distinguish accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scoped arrangements when selecting actions. We develop a controlled benchmark to test whether agents can tell the difference between proposals users have accepted and those they have not, and whether they apply accepted arrangements only where appropriate. Across multiple agents and memory systems, we find that strong memory performance does not ensure Grounding Awareness. More surprisingly, providing more complete user information can increase execution of unacknowledged proposals, while persistent memory can cause agents to treat these proposals as if they were user instructions. We trace these failures through memory writing, retrieval, and action selection. Finally, we introduce Grounding Layer, a lightweight, training-free extension that explicitly tracks grounding status and checks consequential actions, substantially improving agent behavior without modifying models or memory systems.

title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
summary: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

title: AMemOps: Evaluating Memory Updates in Long Audio Streams
summary: Audio memory must recognise recurring sources across acoustic changes while keeping their attributes up to date. Overall accuracy does not reveal how these demands interact. We introduce Audio Memory Operations (AMemOps), a benchmark for latest-attribute retrieval, preservation of unchanged attributes and absent-source rejection in long audio streams. Paired controls vary recordings, training identities and earlier events to examine their effects on updating. Training on other recordings of the test instruments increases a reference delta-rule memory's update advantage over matched attention by 13.4 percentage points. At retrieval delays of 120\,s, matched histories separate benefits of consistent repetition from costs of conflicting earlier values, while additive-memory controls identify benefits of erasure.

summary: A robot's world model must remember objects that leave the camera's view. FloWM, a learned world model, keeps them in a spatial grid of features that it moves with five built-in velocities. FloWM also scores 8 points higher in view although no frame is shown, which we attribute to its write-back of its own predictions. Out of view, the tracker reaches FloWM's range in 14KB against 5.6MB, with no probe. On diagonal motion, outside its five velocities, FloWM finds 11% of blocks even after fine-tuning, while the unchanged tracker keeps 93%. title: Geometric Calibration of Supervised Fine-Tuning
summary: Recent studies investigate the weight geometry through its spectral structure, which characterizes how the weights transform different input directions. Within this view, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is shown to induce dense updates that perturb the spectral geometry of pre-SFT weights along their principal directions, potentially disrupting the model's prior knowledge. These observations motivate using the geometry of pre-SFT weights as a reference for refining learned SFT updates. We study this perspective as Geometric Calibration and develop SPACE Subspace Projection for Adapted Checkpoint Enhancement), a lightweight post-hoc method that selectively reverts SFT update components within the principal subspace of the pre-SFT weights while preserving those in its orthogonal complement. SPACE is a data-free, training-free method that requires only the pre- and post-SFT checkpoints. We evaluate SPACE on Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Qwen3.5, Llama-3.1, and Olmo-3 models ranging from 2B to 14B, across mathematical, coding, and medical SFT, as well as several SFT variants. Overall, SPACE mitigates out-of-domain (OOD) capability regression while further improving in-domain (ID) performance over the uncalibrated SFT checkpoints. For math SFT, SPACE yields average ID/OOD gains of 2.85/2.26 points on Qwen2.5-7B, and 2.41/1.52 points on Qwen3-14B-Base, respectively. These results highlight how the geometric relationship between SFT updates and pre-SFT weights shapes the adapted model's capabilities and, more broadly, motivate geometry-aware parameter updates for continual model improvement.

title: Fairness under Prediction Error in Predict-then-Optimize Pipelines
summary: Fairness constraints in predict-then-optimize pipelines are necessarily enforced on predicted outcomes $\hat{y}$, since true outcomes $y$ are unobserved at decision time. We study whether a demographic parity constraint enforced this way continues to hold against $y$, and how the resulting violation scales with prediction error. Using a budget-constrained allocation problem solved as a linear program, we show empirically that the true-outcome fairness gap grows with prediction error $σ$ and saturates, well fit by $c(1 - e^{-σ/τ})$ with $c = 0.1545 \pm 0.0103$ and $τ= 3.9045 \pm 0.3745$; its mean is invariant to sample size while its variance decays at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{n})$ rate. We derive a two-part theoretical bound: a closed-form local sensitivity result showing the gap's first-order response to prediction error depends on only two individuals per group, validated against the solver to within three significant figures; and a universal, error-independent ceiling following from the boundedness of the decision variable, confirmed consistent with but looser than the empirical saturation level. On US Census income data, enforcing demographic parity on a trained predictor's output reduces an unconstrained disparity in true income to roughly one-third of its original size, leaving 34.4% $\pm$ 3.3% (California) and 35.7% $\pm$ 1.8% (Texas) of the disparity intact and undetectable from the predictions alone -- consistent not only in mechanism but in approximate magnitude across two states with different demographics and income distributions, and stable across ten independent train/test splits in each. A fairness constraint that appears fully satisfied at decision time can mask a substantial, systematic violation of the outcome it was meant to protect.

title: Steering the Fidelity in State Preparation on Noisy Bosonic Systems with Risk-Seeking Optimization
summary: In order to execute quantum algorithms on bosonic quantum computers, it is necessary to encode their inputs into a desired target quantum state, with a process called state preparation. In real settings, state preparation methods operate in stochastic scenarios, where the prepared state is represented as a mixed state, that is a probabilistic ensemble of pure states. Therefore, existing state preparation methods optimize a variational ansatz by averaging over all possible sequences of photon loss events contained in the prepared ensemble, yielding an output state which approximates the desired target with a certain average fidelity. Such an approach, however, does not take into account directly the distribution of fidelities across states in the ensemble. In this work, we aim to maximize the fidelity of only a subset of pure states sampled from the prepared ensemble, at the cost of reducing the average fidelity overall. This trade-off is relevant when the goal is to obtain high-fidelity states with a certain probability, rather than maximizing the average fidelity of the prepared ensemble. We borrow and adapt objective functions from risk-sensitive optimization, a framework that optimizes specific characteristics of a distribution rather than only its expectation, and that has been successfully applied in Reinforcement Learning. In the considered experimental settings, our results show that the infidelities of some pure states in the prepared ensemble can be reduced by up to four orders of magnitude when using risk-seeking objectives, compared to those achieved using the standard optimization of the average fidelity. Furthermore, we show that it is possible to control the trade-off between the probability of obtaining high-fidelity states and the lowest infidelity threshold reached, providing the flexibility to select the operating point that best suits a certain application.

title: Simplifying and Improving On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Diffusion
summary: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.
